description:
Longitudinal archive of the chainsaw suites' published diagnostics grammar in ppat/homelab-ops-kubernetes-apps -- READY, MODE, PULL, CONTENTION, RESTART, UNCENSORED -- kept past the 90 days GitHub retains job logs. Fed by the ci-diagnostics CronJob, which pulls from the GitHub Actions API. Nothing is pushed from CI; there is no inbound path.

BUILT FOR THEN, NOT FOR NOW. Every panel here is a weekly or 28-day aggregate, because the questions this archive exists to answer get asked in six months. Set the range to straddle a change and read across it. The four rows are the four questions, in the order someone reaches for them: did my change help; when did it start getting worse and what moved; what is about to break; and can I trust a comparison across this range at all.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. Pass/fail precision -- `ci/scripts/baseline-census.sh` computes rates from job metadata that outlives logs and classifies ceiling kills properly; the rate panel here exists to share an axis with the other series, not to be exact. And per-run detail and raw line dumps. Explore does that better -- start from `{job="ci-diagnostics"}` and filter by `suite` and `instrument`. A panel that reproduces Explore badly is worse than a link.

HOW TO READ A PANEL. Every description answers three things in order: what you are looking at, what a change in it means, and what would make you act. Where a panel has a known trap -- a denominator that moves on its own, a value that is subtracted rather than observed, a sample too small to resolve what it appears to show -- the trap is in the description, because that is where you meet it.

THE FOUR THINGS MOST LIKELY TO MISLEAD YOU. **A young series looks broken** -- a few hours of data on a 90-day axis is a hairline at the right edge; narrow the range. **Comparability** -- GitHub's runner fleet is heterogeneous and does not say so; measured over six hours, `nproc` was uniformly 4 while the actual CPUs were five different models. Check the CPU stat before believing a small difference. **Population** -- `schedule` is the controlled sample; everything else is contaminated by whatever the branch changed. **Activity is not quality** -- suites are path-filtered on PR, so a suite's run count rises when someone works on it. Every aggregation here is a rate, a quantile or a mean for that reason; a raw total would move with attention rather than with reliability.

Deliberately no alert rules, per the standing no-alerting-until-AI-triage doctrine. The liveness stats at the top are the detection mechanism, not a backstop to one.

panels.title: Can this page be believed right now? (ignores every filter)

panels.description:
**What this is.** One entry per (run, attempt, job) scraped from the GitHub Actions API.

**What a change means.** This is the only panel that separates *a quiet fleet* from *a dead ingester*. Every other panel on this page renders identically in both cases, so a reading of zero invalidates the entire page rather than telling you CI was calm.

**When to act.** Below ~60 for a full day. The scheduled fleet alone is 16 suites x 4 slots, so a healthy day cannot be much lower even with no PR activity. At zero, the CronJob has not written: `kubectl -n ci-diagnostics get cronjob ci-diagnostics`, then the last Job's logs.

A count is the right shape here even though counts move with activity, because the question is binary -- is anything arriving -- not comparative.

targets.expr: sum(count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome"}[24h])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Jobs ingested, last 24h

panels.description:
**What this is.** How many distinct suites appear in the last day.

**What a change means.** It catches the failure a count cannot: a pass that died halfway leaves a healthy-looking total with some suites missing entirely. On a per-suite chart that absence draws as a gap, which reads as *this suite did not run* rather than *we failed to collect it* -- the two have opposite implications and look the same.

**When to act.** A drop that persists across several hours. A single low reading is normal; not every suite runs every day, since PR runs are path-filtered and only the 16 baseline suites are sampled on schedule. 16-17 is healthy.

targets.expr: count(sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome"}[24h]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: Suites seen, last 24h

panels.description:
**What this is.** How many different runner CPUs produced the data you are about to compare.

**What a change means -- and this is the number that most often invalidates a conclusion.** GitHub's hosted fleet is heterogeneous and it does not tell you. Measured over six hours on this repo: `nproc` was uniformly 4 -- so any core-count check reports one configuration, perfectly comparable -- while the actual CPUs were **five different models**, mixing AMD EPYC 7763, EPYC 9V74 and three Intel Xeon generations. A before/after spanning that is comparing machines as well as code, and single-digit-percent differences in pull time or phase duration are not distinguishable from which box you drew.

**When to act.** Any reading above 1 means treat small differences on this page as unresolved. To make a comparison properly, narrow the range until this reads 1, or accept that you are measuring the fleet as well as the change.

A `?` value means `/proc/cpuinfo` carried no `model name` on that runner; the field falls back rather than guessing.

Deliberately not built on `calib_ms`, which looks like the obvious CPU proxy: it is a relative index tied to a fixed iteration count, so editing that count silently rebases the entire historical series.

targets.expr: count(sum by (cpu_model) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention"}[30d]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: Distinct host CPUs in the last 30d

panels.description:
**What this is.** Runs that **succeeded** but did not leave the diagnostics they must -- a healthy run always emits a `CONTENTION start`, a `CONTENTION end` and at least one `READY`.

**What a change means.** A suite whose instrumentation broke contributes no PULL, MODE or READY samples, so its curves above flatten or vanish -- and **every panel then reads as an improvement**. This is the panel that stops the rest of the page lying by omission.

**When to act.** Any non-zero reading, because it should be zero. Find the run and read its `instrumentation` field: `no-lines` means nothing was emitted, `partial` means some prefixes are missing.

Restricted to successes deliberately -- a run that fails before anything becomes Ready legitimately emits no READY, so counting failures would light this up on ordinary red runs and make the one indicator the page depends on into noise. `assertion-semantics` is excluded by name: it pins chainsaw's semantics rather than deploying a module and emits none of the grammar by design.

targets.expr: sum(count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite!="assertion-semantics"} | outcome = "success" | instrumentation =~ "no-lines|partial" [24h])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Passing runs with broken instrumentation, 24h
1. I changed something -- did it help?

panels.description:
**What this is.** Weekly p90 of two numbers per pulled image. `pull_s` is the kubelet's own pull duration; `incl_wait_s` adds the time spent queued behind the kubelet's serial pull queue (`serializeImagePulls: true` in the kind node image).

**What a change means -- read the gap, not either line.** The gap *is* queueing. If the upper line falls toward the lower one and the lower barely moves, the queue was the wall and parallelism removed it: that is the change working. If both fall together, the registry or the network got faster and nothing about the cluster changed. If the lower line rises while the gap shrinks, that is **also success** -- with parallel pulls each individual pull is slower under contention while the set finishes earlier, so `pull_s` alone reads like a regression when the change helped.

**When to act.** A sustained widening of the gap means image pulls are re-serialising -- check node count and the parallel-pull setting. A rise in the *lower* line with a stable gap is not yours to fix; it is upstream.

**Trap.** Cached images emit `PULL-CACHED` and no `PULL` line at all, so a week with more caching shows *fewer* pulls rather than faster ones. A fall here with no other change may be a cache-hit change, not a speed change.

p90 not mean: pull time is long-tailed and the tail is what expires a budget. Weekly not daily: at four scheduled runs per suite per day a daily p90 is mostly noise.

defaults.noValue: No PULL lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top before reading this as a change.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="pull", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap incl_wait_s [7d]) by ()
quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="pull", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap pull_s [7d]) by ()

panels.title: Image pull cost: is the kubelet queue still the wall?

panels.description:
**What this is.** Weekly median of how far into each run the shared prerequisite phase finished -- the `T0+` offset at which `kustomization/flux-system/pre-requisites` became Ready.

**What a change means.** This phase is the dominant cost in most suites, so it is where fixture work shows up and where a chart bump in cert-manager or external-secrets shows up first. A step down after a merge is the fixture change landing. A slow upward drift with no merge behind it is usually an upstream image getting heavier.

**When to act.** A step change you cannot attribute to a landing marker. Then go to *time-to-ready by component* below, which says which component moved.

**Trap, and it limits what you may compare this to.** `T0` is the earliest Ready transition in that run's own list, not the suite's start. These offsets are comparable *between runs of the same suite* and are **not** subtractable from job duration or the chainsaw phase. The decomposition panel below is the one that reconciles clocks properly.

Median not p90, because this phase is bimodal: a high quantile mostly reports which mode won rather than how long the phase took. The mode split is its own panel.

defaults.noValue: No prerequisite READY lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.5, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | name="pre-requisites" | kind="kustomization" | unwrap t0_s [7d]) by (suite)

panels.title: Prerequisite phase duration by suite

panels.description:
**What this is.** Every MODE line's `ctrl_webhook_gap_s`, as a density map -- one column per day, 5-second rows, colour is how many runs landed in that band.

**What a change means.** The claim this panel exists to test is that the gap is bimodal: roughly 20-26s or 75-97s with *zero* intermediates across every run ever classified. No resource story produces that -- contention gives continua and heavy tails, not two clean bands with an empty gulf. So the shape is the finding, and there are three distinct things to watch: whether the **bands move** (something changed in the certificate bootstrap), whether the **slow band gets heavier** (the race is being lost more often), and whether the **middle ever fills in**.

**When to act.** A single point in the 36-59s gap is worth stopping for: **it would falsify the quantizer explanation the whole slow-mode analysis rests on.** A heavier slow band is a regression in the race, not in the timer.

**Trap: colour is a count, so a busy week is a hot week.** Compare the *distribution within a column* against other columns, not the absolute colour across them. The mode-share panel beside this one is the activity-normalised view.

LogQL has no histogram, so this is `max_over_time` per step with Grafana bucketing. Colliding samples show only the larger, which can hide a fast run but cannot manufacture an intermediate one -- so it cannot produce a false refutation. `mode=none` runs carry `ctrl_webhook_gap_s=-` and are excluded; that is not a measurement.

targets.expr: max_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="mode", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | mode != "none" | ctrl_webhook_gap_s != "-" | unwrap ctrl_webhook_gap_s [$__interval]) by (suite)

panels.title: Controller -> webhook gap: are the two bands still two bands?

panels.description:
**What this is.** The fraction of runs in each mode per week -- `fast` (<=35s), `slow` (>=60s), `intermediate` (the 36-59s band), `none` (no external-secrets fixture, or the pods never became Ready).

**What a change means.** A rising `slow` share means the certificate race is being lost more often. Because the penalty is a fixed quantum rather than a continuum, this is the panel that tracks flake exposure: slow mode can run long enough to expire a budget, so share here translates fairly directly into failure risk.

**When to act.** A `slow` share trending up over weeks, or **any** `intermediate` appearing -- no run has ever produced one, and one would mean the two-band model is wrong.

**A share, not a count, and that is a correction.** An earlier version stacked raw counts, which meant the height tracked how busy the fleet was: suites are path-filtered on PR, so a suite being worked on lifts the whole stack while the fast/slow ratio -- the actual question -- is unchanged.

**Trap the share introduces in exchange.** A week with two runs can read 50% slow. Cross-check against the heatmap beside it, where a thin column is visibly thin.

defaults.noValue: No MODE lines in range. Note these only exist on runs after apps#3738 landed.

targets.expr: sum by (mode) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="mode", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" [7d])) / on() group_left sum(count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="mode", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" [7d]))

panels.title: Prerequisite mode share
2. It got worse -- when did it start, and what moved?

panels.description:
**What this is.** A real decomposition: `setup + prerequisite + validates + teardown` sums to the job's wall clock. Height is the job; each band is where the time went.

**What a change means -- this is the panel that localises a regression.** A rising `setup` band is checkout, mise, `kind create` or `flux install`, none of which live in this repo. A rising `prerequisite` band is the shared fixture stack. A rising `validates` band is the suite's own assertions -- the only band whose cause is in the module under test. `teardown` is normally seconds; if it grows, something is not shutting down.

**When to act.** Whichever band grew tells you which repo to open. If `validates` grew, go to *time-to-ready by component* for the specific object.

**What it already shows.** Prerequisite dominates: measured at 181-184s of a 183-205s chainsaw phase, with validates at 2-21s. That is the core mechanic -- Flux applies the whole module at once, so whatever asserts first absorbs the convergence and everything after it returns instantly. It also means a *validates* number is not a measure of that assertion's cost.

**Trap: a band that thins may mean 'underivable', not 'faster'.** A phase that could not be derived is absent, never zero -- a ceiling-killed run emits none of the grammar, and a run whose prerequisites never reached `Ready: True` has no prerequisite boundary. Those jobs still contribute setup/chainsaw/teardown. Check the broken-instrumentation stat before reading a thinning band as an improvement.

Means, not medians: means are additive so the bands sum to the total, while a stack of medians would draw a total no run ever had. Computed at ingest from three absolute clocks, each field recording its origin; `validates_s` is a subtraction, not an observation. `residual_s` is emitted as a self-check and is 0 on every job measured.

defaults.noValue: No PHASE records yet. These are derived at ingest and only exist for jobs collected after clusters#939 deployed.

targets.expr: avg_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="phase", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | setup_s != "" | unwrap setup_s [7d]) by ()
avg_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="phase", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | prerequisite_s != "" | unwrap prerequisite_s [7d]) by ()
avg_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="phase", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | validates_s != "" | unwrap validates_s [7d]) by ()
avg_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="phase", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | teardown_s != "" | unwrap teardown_s [7d]) by ()

panels.title: Where a job's time goes

panels.description:
**What this is.** Weekly p90 of how long each component took to become Ready, grouped by kind and namespace. One entry per pod, Kustomization and HelmRelease per run.

**What a change means.** This is the *what moved* to the decomposition panel's *which phase moved*. A single namespace stepping up while the rest are flat is a chart bump or an image getting heavier in that component. Everything rising together is the runner or the network, not the component.

**When to act.** A namespace that steps up and stays up. This is the earliest available signal -- it moves before a budget expires and long before anything goes red, which is the whole reason to keep it.

**Trap.** Grouped by namespace rather than object name, because pod names carry two random suffixes and grouping by name would mint a new series per run and exceed the series limit. So a namespace running several components shows the slowest of them, not each.

Same `T0` caveat as elsewhere: offsets compare between runs of a suite, not against job duration. Narrow `suite` to one value before reading absolute numbers.

defaults.noValue: No READY lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | unwrap t0_s [7d]) by (kind, namespace)

panels.title: Time-to-ready by component

panels.description:
**What this is.** Non-success outcomes over all outcomes, per suite, on a 28-day rolling window.

**What a change means.** A level that holds for months is a real change in reliability. Movement between adjacent points is mostly sampling: a 28-day point is about **n=112**, and a true 10% rate at n=112 has a 95% interval of roughly **5% to 17%** -- so 8% to 14% is noise, not a signal.

**When to act.** A sustained level shift, cross-checked against the denominator beside it. For an exact rate use `ci/scripts/baseline-census.sh`, which reads job metadata that outlives logs and classifies ceiling kills properly; **this panel is for correlation with the other series on the same axis, not for precision.**

**Trap: the denominator moves on its own.** Suites are path-filtered on PR, so a suite's run count rises when someone works on it -- and a rate can shift with no change in reliability at all. Read the panel beside this one before believing a move.

`outcome` is the discriminated field, not GitHub's raw conclusion, so a ceiling kill (`timed_out`) is separable from a concurrency cancel (`superseded`). **`superseded` counts as a failure**, which overstates the rate on busy PR days -- set the population to `schedule` to remove that entirely.

defaults.noValue: No OUTCOME samples in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome != "success" [28d])) / sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" [28d]))

panels.title: Failure rate by suite, rolling 28d

panels.description:
**What this is.** The denominator of the panel beside it -- how many outcomes each 28-day point is computed from, per suite.

**What a change means.** A rate whose denominator is also moving changed for reasons of sampling, not quality. This is the panel that tells the two apart, and it is the reason the rate panel was cut once already.

**When to act.** Treat any rate movement whose denominator moved with it as unproven. Below about 30 runs, read the rate as a direction rather than a number.

targets.expr: sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="outcome", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" [28d]))

panels.title: Runs behind each rate point
3. What is about to break?

panels.description:
**What this is.** The share of a suite's `READY` records that were **not** `True` on runs that **succeeded**. Something in the cluster never converged and the suite passed regardless.

**What a change means.** There are only two explanations and you need to know which:

- **Nothing asserts on that object** -- a coverage gap. The suite is green because it never looked. Nothing will ever catch a regression there.
- **Something does assert on it, and is riding on generous budget** -- headroom being eaten. The run passed on timing it did not have much of.

Tell them apart by finding the object in the suite's `validate-*.yaml`: if it is named, you are in the second case.

**When to act.** A rising share, or a new `kind` appearing. **This is where the next flake comes from** -- it is the only leading indicator on the page, because it fires while runs are still passing. Everything in the UNCENSORED panel beside it has already failed.

The discriminator this rests on: **`Ready: Unknown` means under-budgeted; `Ready: False` with a reason means broken.** A real example already in the data -- `apps-ai`, a successful scheduled run, `kustomization/flux-system/pre-requisites` at `Ready: Unknown` with `t0_s=424`.

**A share, not a count.** Counts here moved with fleet activity, so a suite being worked on looked like it was degrading. Normalised against that suite's own READY volume.

defaults.noValue: Nothing was left un-Ready on a passing run -- good news, provided the liveness stats at the top are non-zero.

targets.expr: sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome="success" | ready_state != "True" [7d])) / sum by (suite) (count_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="ready", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | outcome="success" [7d]))

panels.title: Latent risk: things never became Ready and the suite passed anyway

panels.description:
**What this is.** After a suite goes red, a watch keeps observing and records how much longer each not-Ready object actually took. Ranked by that figure, worst first.

**Why this is the most valuable data on the page.** Budgets are sized `observed_max x 3` **from green runs only** -- because every timeout failure is censored at its own budget, so an assert dying at 60.0s of a 60s budget tells you nothing about what it needed. The x3 comes from cost asymmetry, not from evidence. **`UNCENSORED` is the only data that can size a budget from evidence**, and these numbers are what to use instead of the multiplier.

**What a value means -- and this is the thing readers get wrong.** A number here means **the budget was too tight by roughly that much. It does not mean the component is broken.** Broken leaves obligatory evidence behind: `CrashLoopBackOff`, non-zero restarts, `Helm install failed`, an Error event. The *absence* of that evidence is what distinguishes late from broken, and if it is absent the fix is the budget.

**When to act.** Take the top rows to the suite's budget for that step and add the observed figure rather than a multiple. `never` is the exception: on a CNPG `Cluster` it is a real bug (#3678), not a tight budget -- do not raise a budget to make it green.

**Trap.** The grammar records **objects**, not step names, and carries no budgets at all -- those live in the suite YAML. So this ranks *what needed time*, not *which assertion is closest to expiring*. The panel beside it is the closer thing to that.

These live almost entirely on PR failures, so the population filter deliberately does not reach this panel -- filtering it would leave it empty on nearly every visit, and empty would read as 'nothing needed extra time'.

targets.expr: topk(20, max by (suite, kind, namespace, name) (max_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="uncensored", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | extra_s != "" | unwrap extra_s [$__range])))

panels.title: How much longer a wait actually needed than its budget allowed

panels.description:
**What this is.** One row per container that restarted inside an assertion's budget, per week. A cell exists if that container restarted at all that week; colour is the mean restarts per occurrence.

**What a change means -- and the primary signal is a new row appearing, not a colour.** This estate deliberately tolerates longhorn's crash-restart cycle, and the stated reason that tolerance is safe is that restart counts stay visible on green runs. So there are two questions: *is the tolerated defect still bounded* (colour on an existing row) and *has something new started restarting* (a row that was not there before). **The second matters more**, because a container crashing inside a budget is invisible everywhere else -- the suite still passes and the pod still reports Ready.

**When to act.** A container name you do not recognise, immediately. A known row getting darker means the tolerated cycle is worsening and the tolerance needs revisiting.

**Why a timeline rather than a graph.** A weekly *total* was the obvious chart and it was wrong: suites are path-filtered on PR, so a total rises when someone works on a suite while reliability is unchanged. And a curve buries the thing that matters -- a new series appearing is far more legible as a new row than as another line in a crowded legend.

**Trap.** Grouped by container, not pod: pod names carry random suffixes and would mint a new series per run. Two different components with the same container name would merge.

targets.expr: avg by (container) (avg_over_time({job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="restart", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | container != "" | unwrap restarts [7d]))

panels.title: Which containers crashed inside a budget -- a new row is the alarm
4. Can I trust a comparison across this range?

panels.description:
**What this is.** Two probes per run -- one at the start of the chainsaw phase, one at the end, never in between, because a bandwidth probe fired mid-run would *be* the contention it claims to measure. Drawn as the weekly floor of throughput and the weekly peak of fsync latency.

**What a change means.** Bandwidth is the axis measured to matter: a 150mbit shaped link reproduced the failures 6/6 on the rig, while halving cluster CPU changed nothing. So a week where the **throughput floor collapsed** is a week whose pull times and phase durations mean something different -- the numbers above are not wrong, they are answering a different question. `fsync_us` is here for elimination rather than as an established cause; it is the untested candidate for the prerequisite phase's bimodality.

**When to act.** Do not act on this panel; use it to *discount* movement elsewhere. If a regression above coincides with a throughput collapse here, you have not found a regression, you have found a bad week on the fleet.

**Trap: this does not establish comparability.** It describes conditions, not hardware. Two runs with identical throughput on different CPU models are still not comparable -- that is what the CPU stat at the top of the page is for.

`calib_ms` is deliberately absent from this entire page: a relative index tied to a fixed iteration count, so editing that count silently rebases the whole series -- a step change indistinguishable from a real one, which a multi-year archive cannot survive.

defaults.noValue: No CONTENTION lines in range. Check the liveness stats at the top.

targets.expr: quantile_over_time(0.1, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | net_mbps =~ "[0-9].*" | unwrap net_mbps [7d]) by ()
quantile_over_time(0.9, {job="ci-diagnostics", instrument="contention", suite=~"^(${suite:regex})$"} | gh_event=~"^(${population:regex})$" | fsync_us =~ "[0-9].*" | unwrap fsync_us [7d]) by ()

panels.title: Runner conditions at the two run boundaries

list.description: Which Loki to read. The value is the datasource UID, not its display name.
list.label: Datasource
list.name: datasource

list.description:
Which chainsaw suites to include. Reaches every panel except the liveness stats at the top and the UNCENSORED ranking, which deliberately ignore it.

What makes All safe is `allValue: .*`, not the anchoring -- the two pull opposite ways. An empty selection matches nothing (`^()$` matches only the empty string) and renders an empty page rather than an error. If everything is blank, check this before concluding the ingester stopped.
list.label: Suite
list.name: suite

list.description:
Which population of runs to read. **The most consequential control here.**

`schedule` is the designed sample: sixteen suites, four fixed slots a day, always `main`, with suite content that only changes when someone merges. It is the only population in which a before/after means anything.

`pull_request` runs execute arbitrary branch code -- a PR that changes a suite's budgets or node count moves the very numbers being trended -- and `push` runs are path-filtered, so a suite is sampled more often precisely when it is being worked on. Pooling either into a trend is the contaminated measurement this series exists to replace.

It deliberately does not reach the UNCENSORED ranking, which lives almost entirely on PR failures and would be empty on nearly every visit.
list.label: Population
list.name: population

title: CI Suite Diagnostics
